newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan pressure groups hedge bets on elections.
newsitem.headline: Japan pressure groups hedge bets on elections.

text.p: Japan's powerful business, labour and farm pressure groups, for decades key vote-collecting machines, are this time hedging their bets on who will win Sunday's general election.
Analysts say the pressure groups, wary of backing the wrong horse in one of Japan's most unpredictable elections ever, are contributing campaign funds across the political spectrum.
The tactic is a major shift from their traditional strategy of each backing just one party.
"They are trying to hedge their risks because they could be in trouble or at least powerless if parties they don't support form a government," said political analyst Minoru Morita.
The lineup previously was that business groups and farmers backed the conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) while unions sided with the Social Democrats and small leftist parties.
But this time, business groups have avoided official support for any party, simply saying they prefer parties that are serious about economic deregulation and tax and administrative reforms.

Shoichiro Toyoda, head of the powerful Japan Federation of Economic Organisations (Keidanren), sent letters this week to the country's top 1,230 firms, urging employers and employees to go to the polls. But he endorsed no specific party.
But if big business's official stance is neutral, analysts say it is giving behind-the-scenes support to the LDP and the main opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party).
Morita said business groups and farmers secretly hoped for an LDP win as they believed this would stabilise politics.
Trade unions are having a harder time deciding.

The Japanese Trade Union Confederation (Rengo), the country's largest labour grouping with 7.8 million members, is split into two main camps -- one supporting the new Democratic Party and the other favouring Shinshinto.
But in the intricate world of Japanese politics, some small unions in Rengo are "secretly" backing at least 60 candidates running on the LDP ticket, one labour source said.
Political analysts said the formerly strong influence of trade unions on politics had waned.

"The strength of trade unions has been reduced to a mere skeleton," said Tadashi Iyasu, a professor at Ryukoku University in the city of Otsu in southwestern Japan. "That's why the Socialists are in miserable shape now."
Morita said: "The trade unions used to be staunch backers of opposition parties, not ruling parties."
Most analysts say the LDP is doing best in the pressure groups stakes and is on course to win a clear majority in the 500-seat Lower House.

"The LDP's increased seats will be accompanied by an increase in the number of interest groups that will want to collect favours from legislators," said Takayoshi Miyagawa, head of the Centre for Political Public Relations.
"Japan's politics will be no different from what they used to be several years ago," Morita said. "That's bad for Japan."
